title: "These Are My Jewels"
text:
Cornelia was the daughter of Scipio Africanus, the general who defeated Hannibal. Widowed young, she refused to remarry (Plutarch says she even turned down a proposal from a king of Egypt) and devoted herself to raising her children. Of twelve, only three survived to adulthood, among them Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, who later became famous as reforming tribunes of the people.

Valerius Maximus, who collected memorable deeds and sayings for Roman readers in the first century AD, tells how a wealthy woman from Campania once stayed as a guest in Cornelia's house. The visitor showed off her jewelry, which was the most beautiful of its time. Cornelia kept her talking until her sons came home from school. Then she pointed to them and said: "These are my jewels."

Cornelia was known in Rome for her education and her letters, and Cicero and Quintilian both said her sons owed their fine speech to her. Plutarch writes that she took care to raise them so well that they were thought to owe their virtue more to their education than to their birth. After both sons were killed in political violence, she lived on at Misenum, receiving visitors and speaking of her sons without tears, Plutarch says, as she would speak of the heroes of old.
lesson: What we pour into our children's character is worth more than anything we can display. Time and attention spent on their education is an investment no jewel can match.
source: Valerius Maximus, Memorable Deeds and Sayings 4.4 (preface); Plutarch, Life of Tiberius Gracchus 1 and Life of Gaius Gracchus 19
